words.title: Almah, betulah, parthenos

forms.g: A young woman of marriageable age (Masoretic text).
The specific Hebrew word for virgin.
Virgin. The Septuagint’s rendering of almah.

excerpt: They did the same in Isaiah 7:14. The Masoretic Hebrew word is almah, a young woman of marriageable age. Not betulah, the specific Hebrew word for virgin. The Septuagint translated almah as parthenos, virgin. Matthew 1:23 quotes the Greek. The virgin birth as christological proof rests on the Septuagintal reading, not the Masoretic Hebrew.

words.title: Ka’ari and oruxan

forms.g: Like a lion (Masoretic text).
They dug, or they pierced (Septuagint).

excerpt: The Masoretic Hebrew does not say “they pierced.” It says “like a lion at my hands and my feet,” a construction with no functioning verb, a phrase that breaks grammatically and produces no coherent image. The word is ka’ari, like a lion. The verb “pierced” belongs to the Septuagint, where the Greek oruxan means “they dug” or “they pierced.”
words.en: Like a lion, or they pierced

words.title: Heteras

forms.g: Other, different, of another kind.

excerpt: The Greek word heteras means “other, different, of another kind.” What kind? The same categorical difference Genesis 6 describes: human plus non-human.

words.title: Pharmakeia

forms.g: Sorcery. Literally the use of drugs or substances for spiritual purposes.

excerpt: Pharmakeia, the Greek word for “sorcery” in Revelation 18, literally “the use of drugs/substances for spiritual purposes,” describes substance-based rewiring of human neurochemistry.

words.title: Tsela

forms.g: Does not always mean “rib.”

excerpt: The Hebrew word tsela does not always mean “rib.” No one serious disputes that. But words are not translated from dictionaries. They are translated from context.

words.title: To’evah

forms.g: Abomination. A legal term, used in Leviticus 18:22.

excerpt: They committed abominations: The Hebrew word to'evah—the same legal term used in Leviticus 18:22. Not the only charge, but absolutely part of the indictment.

words.title: Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, Tartarus

forms.g: The land of the dead.
The Septuagint’s word for Sheol.
One of four terms English renders with the same word.
Appears once, as a verb, in 2 Peter 2:4: a holding cell for the sinning angels.

excerpt: Tartarus shows up exactly once, as a verb, when Peter says God cast the sinning angels down to hold them for judgment (2 Peter 2:4). He borrowed the word from Greek myth to describe a holding cell, not a headquarters.
Hades, in Greek, is what the Septuagint uses to translate Sheol. Same idea in a new language. The land of the dead, not a torture chamber with a warden.
English translators then used that single inherited word for Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, and Peter’s verb tartaroō. Four biblical terms entered the English imagination wearing the same name.

words.title: Nephesh and psyche

forms.g: The whole living creature: breath and blood and ground held together.
In Platonic philosophy, the immortal rational soul housed in corruptible matter.

excerpt: The vocabulary swap was subtle and devastating. The Hebrew nephesh became the Greek psyche. On paper it looks like straightforward translation. In practice it was category replacement. Nephesh in Hebrew is the whole living creature, breath and blood and ground held together. Psyche in Platonic philosophy is the immortal rational soul temporarily housed in corruptible matter. When the Septuagint translated nephesh as psyche, it baptized the Platonic frame into the Hebrew text.
words.en: Soul: the living creature, or the immortal soul

words.title: Ekklesia, presbyteros, metanoia

forms.g: Tyndale rendered it “congregation,” not “church.”
Tyndale rendered it “elder,” not “priest.”
Tyndale rendered it “repentance,” not “penance.”

excerpt: The translation itself was not neutral work. It never is. Every translator makes choices, and Tyndale’s choices were arguments. He rendered the Greek ekklesia as “congregation” rather than “church.” He rendered presbyteros as “elder” rather than “priest.” He rendered metanoia as “repentance” rather than “penance.” Each of these choices collapsed a piece of the institutional scaffolding. Penance required a priest. A priest required a hierarchy. A hierarchy required Rome.

words.title: Cherem

forms.g: A binding curse. The oath the Watchers swore on Mount Hermon.

excerpt: The conflict began in the heavens. Two hundred celestial beings assigned to watch humanity abandoned their posts. Not impulsively. Strategically. They assembled on Mount Hermon. They swore a mutual oath, Hebrew: cherem, a binding curse. They knew the cost. They accepted it anyway.

words.title: Porneia

forms.g: Sexual immorality. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 5:1 to condemn incest.

excerpt: Progressive Christianity claims porneia only meant temple prostitution or abusive relationships. But Paul uses the same word in 1 Corinthians 5:1 to explicitly condemn incest, a man sleeping with his father’s wife. If you trust the Gospel writers on Jesus’ use of porneia, you are trusting the same transmission stream that preserved Paul’s clarifications.

words.title: Cush

forms.g: The historical land of Ethiopia, a biblical synecdoche for Africa.

excerpt: While Western prophecy teachers fixate on Tel Aviv, the Bible consistently points to another land as the focus of God’s end-time gathering. The prophetic finger points to the land “beyond the rivers of Cush”—the historical land of Ethiopia, a biblical synecdoche for Africa.

tiers.title: New Testament translation tier list
tiers.lede: How much does a translation let the Greek speak, and how much does it let the translators speak instead?
tiers.standard: One question decides every placement: does this translation render what the Greek says, or what the committee thinks the Greek means?

items.t: Word-for-word, with tense, mood and voice kept. It is open-source, so anyone who reads Greek can test its choices. Primary study tool, and the New Testament text in this index.
The most literal mainstream English New Testament, from the critical Greek text. Hard to read devotionally, which the list treats as the point. Primary study tool.
More wooden-literal than the NASB, on the critical text. It comes from John MacArthur’s seminary, and that theology occasionally shows in interpretive choices.
Formal equivalence on the critical text, strong for word-level study. A Reformed committee, and that occasionally shows in passages on grace and works.
The main text favors readable English over strict literalism. Its 60,000-plus translator footnotes document every textual decision. Use it beside the NASB, not instead of it.
Readability was a goal alongside literalism, so the committee smoothed the Greek in places. Solid critical text. For cross-reference, not a primary study Bible.

The English is unmatched, but the base is the Textus Receptus (Erasmus, 1516), built from late manuscripts. It carries 1 John 5:7, Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11, which are not in the oldest manuscripts. Use for rhetorical weight.
The KJV’s English updated, on the same Textus Receptus base. Its footnotes at least show where manuscripts disagree. Same additions, same tier.
The most popular English Bible, and thought-for-thought in method. The committee’s reading of what the text means replaces what it says, and the reader cannot see where.
Mixes word-for-word and thought-for-thought, and the reader cannot tell where the line falls.
Gender-inclusive language in places the Greek does not call for, a modern preference added to an ancient text.
A paraphrase. Fine for introducing the story, not for building doctrine.
A Textus Receptus base like the KJV, without the KJV’s English.
A cultural paraphrase. Some passages work as commentary. It is not a study text.
Adds words and ideas found in no Greek manuscript. Do not use.

use: ESV, with the NET footnotes beside your primary.
You are reading the committee, not the text.

english.title: Reading the Ethiopian books in English
english.lede: No complete, church-approved English translation of all 81 books exists yet. Most of the books a Protestant Bible leaves out can still be read in English, and six of them are here.

items: Reproof. Ethiopian Bibles count the closing chapters of Proverbs as their own book, so the text is in every Bible, inside Proverbs.
Their counterparts are the books of Esdras (1 Esdras, and 2 Esdras, also called 4 Ezra), found in most English Apocrypha.
Ethiopian Meqabyan, not the Greek books of Maccabees. Only a few English translations exist, mostly recent.
Also Meqabyan. English translations are few.
The Ethiopic version of Yosippon, a medieval Hebrew history of the Jews. English versions of the Hebrew exist; the Ethiopic is hard to find.

groups.note: The Sinodos (Sirate Tsion, Tizaz, Gitsew, Abtilis), the Book of the Covenant (1 and 2 Dominos), Clement and the Didascalia. English exists mainly in older scholarly editions and excerpts. Full translations are rare.

english.foot: Ethiopian Bibles also carry 4 Baruch (the Paralipomena of Jeremiah) with Jeremiah. English translations exist in collections of early Jewish writings.

numbering_scope._about: For a book whose verse map is partial, the page warns about unconverted English numbers on every chapter unless the book is listed here. A listed book warns only on the chapters named, because the rest are known to match English numbering. Genesis: 48 of 50 chapters have the same verse count as English Bibles; chapters 31 (54 verses against 55) and 32 (33 against 32) differ, the boundary shift at Jacob's journey (English 32:26 = Septuagint 32:27). Add a book here only after checking its chapters.
